title: The sirens of the AI apocalypse
gist: Philosopher Sasha Mudd argues that the New York Times' optimism that society can restrain AI as it restrained nuclear weapons skips the hard step of recognising catastrophe. Drawing on Günther Anders' 'Promethean gap' and Hannah Arendt, she says abstract AI-extinction risk is poorly imagined while accelerationist utopias are vividly imagined, making pressing ahead look morally courageous.

insights.claim: After Jacob Coxon publicly quit Anthropic warning that many AI builders believe advanced AI could kill us all within the decade, a New York Times editorial argued by analogy with postwar nuclear control that society can restrain dangerous innovation once it decides to.
insights.speaker: Sasha Mudd
insights.so_what: High-profile insider departures are feeding mainstream debate on AI restraint — a regulatory-risk signal for frontier AI labs.
insights.quote: many of the people building advanced AI sincerely believe it could kill us all within the decade

insights.claim: The NYT's optimistic sequence — recognise danger, decide on restraint, coordinate and regulate — omits the prior and fraught step of a society coming to recognise that a promising technology is morally urgent enough to curb; 'once it decides to' does a lot of work.
insights.speaker: Sasha Mudd
insights.so_what: Investors should not assume regulatory restraint on AI will arrive promptly; recognition lags may let development run ahead.
insights.quote: For “once it decides to” is doing rather a lot of work.

insights.claim: Günther Anders argued after Hiroshima that modern technology opened a 'Promethean gap' between what humans can produce and what they can imaginatively comprehend, so people can know propositionally that something could kill everyone yet fail to make it morally real.
insights.speaker: Sasha Mudd
insights.so_what: Explains why public and political pressure on AI existential risk may stay muted relative to its stated severity.
insights.quote: Our powers had become enormous while our moral imaginations remained stubbornly small.
insights.locator: The same postwar history the Times

insights.claim: Bigger catastrophes can be harder, not easier, to fear: one dead child is imaginable, a thousand become a statistic, and human extinction cannot be photographed.
insights.speaker: Sasha Mudd
insights.so_what: Scale of risk does not translate linearly into political mobilisation.
insights.quote: The destruction of a city can be photographed, while the extinction of humanity cannot.

insights.claim: Unlike nuclear war's mushroom clouds or pandemics' hospitals, 'loss of control over superintelligence' is expressed abstractly in terms of model behaviour, probabilities, alignment failures and unprecedented cascading events, so the public's imaginative grasp of the risk remains thin.
insights.speaker: Sasha Mudd
insights.so_what: AI safety lacks a vivid focal image, weakening the political coalition for regulation absent an actual incident.
insights.locator: The existential worry around rogue AI

insights.claim: The upside of AI is richly imagined by accelerationists: cured diseases, the end of work, abundance, leaving Earth and even biology — e.g. Sam Altman on uploading his brain to the cloud, Elon Musk's interplanetary ambitions, and Marc Andreessen's 'technological supermen'.
insights.speaker: Sasha Mudd
insights.so_what: Leaders of major AI capital allocators hold maximalist visions that bias them toward speed over caution.
insights.locator: The other side of the ledger

insights.claim: In the accelerationist imagination the greatest danger is moving too slowly; Andreessen's Techno-Optimist Manifesto states that any deceleration of AI will cost lives, making hesitation itself a source of preventable death.
insights.speaker: Sasha Mudd
insights.so_what: This framing gives industry a moral argument against regulation, sustaining the capex race.
insights.quote: “We believe any deceleration of AI will cost lives.”
insights.locator: The other side of the ledger

insights.claim: The core problem is not a lack of imagination but a clash between two incompatible ways of imagining the end: catastrophe as passage to something greater versus a postwar suspicion of futures grand enough to make present people expendable.
insights.speaker: Sasha Mudd
insights.so_what: AI governance debate is a values clash unlikely to resolve via evidence alone — expect persistent polarisation.
insights.locator: The other side of the ledger

insights.claim: Hannah Arendt's concept of human 'superfluousness', developed about totalitarianism, applies to AI: it asks what happens when an inexorable movement of history matters more than the humans living through it.
insights.speaker: Sasha Mudd
insights.so_what: Frames labour-displacement and existential AI concerns as political legitimacy issues.
insights.locator: The other moral imagination was forged

insights.claim: The postwar principle was not to avoid bold risks, but that the allure of an imagined future cannot alone justify treating people as expendable — a principle harder to uphold when the promised destination is unimaginably grand.
insights.speaker: Sasha Mudd
insights.so_what: The grander AI's promised payoff, the weaker the ethical brake on risk-taking.

insights.claim: Prosaic drivers of continued AI development include money, geopolitical competition, sunk investment, and the argument that if responsible companies stop, irresponsible ones will carry on — but these do not fully explain why pressing ahead seems morally courageous to leaders.
insights.speaker: Sasha Mudd
insights.so_what: Sunk capex and geopolitical race dynamics make voluntary slowdown by AI firms unlikely.
insights.locator: Of course, there are more prosaic

insights.claim: The 20th-century 'Never again' ethic was built from memory, testimony and ruins; AI risk demands recognising catastrophe before such memory exists, without waiting for disaster to supply the lesson.
insights.speaker: Sasha Mudd
insights.so_what: Implies meaningful AI regulation may only arrive after a tangible incident — a tail risk for the sector.
insights.quote: to recognise catastrophe before memory, testimony and ruins have made its meaning vivid for us
insights.locator: Of course, there are more prosaic
